segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: When I was in my 20s, I worked as a temp typist on the overnight shift. And it was one of my favorite jobs I ever had. I showed up at work at midnight. Downtown was completely dark. Nobody on the streets at all. And I'd take the elevator to the, you know, 20th floor or whatever it was. And it would be all lit up and bustling with activity, dozens of people rushing around. Usually we were hustling out some kind of legal brief or exhibit for court the next day.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I loved being up when the rest of the world was asleep. And the next morning, when I would walk to the subway as the sun was coming up, I loved knowing that everybody else on the street was dragging themselves to their jobs and I was done for the day. It was like I was part of a secret society that's alive in the middle of the night.

The whole point of this is do this on a boring Monday or Tuesday or Thursday night. A school night when other people aren't out having fun.

segments.speaker: Friend 1
segments.text: There's no destination. It's basically just glorified cruising. They drive around for hours, talking about whatever, singing along to the music. [SINGING]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: From WBEZ Chicago, it's This American Life, distributed by Public Radio International. I'm Ira Glass.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Today on our show, we spend an hour with the secret society that is up in the middle of the night. All the people doing things that they would never do during the daytime, and the people doing things that they might be during the day that just feel different when you do them at night. Moving products, and hauling across a war zone, and caring for sick kids, and just wandering the streets to get out of the house. Everything is different at night. We witness how in five acts. Stay with us.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Act One. Orange You Glad I Didn't Say Banana?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: To get to the Hunts Point Market, you drive through this industrial part of the South Bronx, and at night, it's abandoned. For miles, you pass all these closed auto repair lots and plumbing supply stores. And then you go through a fence, pass some pretty intense security, drive a bit more, and suddenly, boom. You are in the Hunts Point Terminal Market.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And it's like a busy city at rush hour. Bright and loud. Forklifts whipping around, carrying pallets to trucks. Warehouses in long rows, several city blocks long. 60 acres of produce.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: When people arrive here at 10 PM to work, what they say to each other is "good morning," because the middle of the night is when the most of the business gets done.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Two members of the team of economics reporters at Planet Money, Adam Davidson and Chana Joffe-Walt usually report on financial markets and derivative markets and currency markets, so they were pleased to get a chance to actually visit a market what people buy and sell stuff that you can see and touch and smell. Here they are.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Eddie One-Way needs some pears.

segments.speaker: Adam Davidson
segments.text: His name is actually Edward Joseph. They call him "Eddie One-Way" because he wants prices to go one way-- down. He's a buyer, one of thousands of guys who show up here every night.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: And they're buying for pretty much every grocery store, restaurant, corner market in the northeast. If you have ever bought a Golden Delicious apple or ate a salad in a restaurant between Philly and Boston, chances are it came through here.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: And it is nothing like when you or I buy a salad at a restaurant. There are no posted prices. It us pure supply and demand.

segments.speaker: Adam Davidson
segments.text: And right now, demand-- that's Eddie One-Way, the buyer-- is looking for supply.

segments.speaker: Eddie One-way
segments.text: Let's see here, where's my salesman? Oh, Mr. Timmy?

segments.speaker: Adam Davidson
segments.text: Timmy is a salesman at one of the wholesalers here, to Rigo Brothers.

segments.speaker: Eddie One-way
segments.text: He's close by. I think he's in one of these refrigerators.

segments.speaker: Eddie One-way
segments.text: This place here is a stadium. I think you need GPS to get around here. It would help.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Eventually, Eddie One-Way finds Timmy, and they enter into a ritual that will happen thousands of times throughout the night. They try to negotiate a price.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Eddie thinks $15 for a box of pears seems fair. Timmy doesn't.

segments.speaker: Timmy
segments.text: No way.

segments.speaker: Eddie One-way
segments.text: We could do it--

segments.speaker: Timmy
segments.text: I told you 20 yesterday.

segments.speaker: Eddie One-way
segments.text: Yesterday's gone. Today's a new day.

segments.speaker: Timmy
segments.text: $20 yesterday, 18 today. That's it.

segments.speaker: Eddie One-way
segments.text: Stay close, Timmy.

segments.speaker: Adam Davidson
segments.text: Timmy offers Eddie a different kind of pear for $15, which to me looked exactly the same.

segments.speaker: Eddie One-way
segments.text: $15 on these, $18 on them.

segments.speaker: Adam Davidson
segments.text: But Eddie One-Way knows things about pears that I will never know, and he ignores that ridiculous offer.

segments.speaker: Adam Davidson
segments.text: Why do you want to pay $15? Why is 18--?

segments.speaker: Eddie One-way
segments.text: I'd like to pay 13, but I'm being generous.

segments.speaker: Timmy
segments.text: All right. That's it, brother. That's it, man. 18 is the right number. You know it's what they're worth.

segments.speaker: Eddie One-way
segments.text: The night's still young.

segments.speaker: Adam Davidson
segments.text: Eventually Eddie One-Way walks away. The night is still young. At this hour the sellers, guys like Timmy, feel like they are in control. They don't want to give anything away too cheap yet. There's lots more buyers still to come. But Eddie, the buyer, is hoping that if he comes back later in the night, Timmy won't have sold that much. He'll be desperate to get rid of his pears, and will accept a lower price. But Eddie's really taking a risk here.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: I know. I actually saw this risk play out with carrots, and it was really stressful. Jeff Steinberg is a buyer like Eddie, and he was looking for this one particular kind of carrot. A fancy one. Loose California. And I followed him around, walking the aisles, one seller to another. And at first, everyone has the carrots, but Jeff is offended-- or at least acts offended-- by the high prices. And then an hour passes. And now nobody has Loose Californias anymore. Jeff can't find the carrots he needs at any price. So he's thinking he may have to settle for something inferior-- Loose Canadians.

segments.speaker: Jeff Steinberg
segments.text: Eugh.

segments.speaker: Adam Davidson
segments.text: Jeff asks a seller named Carlos how much for the Loose Canadians. Carlos tells him eight bucks a box.

segments.speaker: Jeff Steinberg
segments.text: I'll be right back, then.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: What's he doing now?

segments.speaker: Carlos
segments.text: Going to look at something that he's going to come back and tell me he doesn't like.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: What does it mean that he's not going to like it?

segments.speaker: Carlos
segments.text: Probably because they're not good enough for his customers. He's fairly picky, so you have to give the right people the right stuff.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: And sure enough, Jeff comes out of the warehouse, shaking his head.

segments.speaker: Jeff Steinberg
segments.text: No good.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: No good? And where are you going to look for carrots next?

segments.speaker: Jeff Steinberg
segments.text: That's a good question, because I've pretty much looked all over the place.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: So it's 11:30 at night, and carrots are your problem at the moment.

segments.speaker: Jeff Steinberg
segments.text: At the moment. It's coming down to that hour where I'm probably going to have to pay what they wanted, what I don't want to pay.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Around midnight, it starts to get hectic. Buyers fill the streets. Sellers wave their arms and yell into faces and cell phones. There's a lot of sweating. And as the minutes pass, all these little stories emerge.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Midnight, the big story-- tomatoes. They're on fire. Yesterday they were selling for $15. Now they're $25. Everyone is buying.

segments.speaker: Adam Davidson
segments.text: Also breaking this hour-- leafy greens from California. They're huge, because as everyone says, they have weather out there. There's not enough leafy greens coming to satisfy the demand.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: It's around this time that we meet Angela Poricelli. Angela is the only woman we see the entire night. She says she knows of only one other woman who works here alongside something like 7,000 men.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Her booth is decorated with pictures. She has a big cross. She brings in fresh flowers every week.

segments.speaker: Adam Davidson
segments.text: She offered me candy. And hanging out with her, we learned that it's not all business here in the middle of the night. We keep seeing her next door neighbor, Henry Polio, stopping by on all sorts of dubious missions. Right now he's looking for a fork.

segments.speaker: Angela Poricelli
segments.text: Hello.

segments.speaker: Henry Polio
segments.text: Do you have a fork?

segments.speaker: Angela Poricelli
segments.text: Yes, I do.

segments.speaker: Henry Polio
segments.text: She's the loveliest woman in the market. Believe me, she's the most wonderful person in the world. I know  who her family is. Our family, grandfathers know grandfathers, fathers knew fathers. Wonderful woman.

segments.speaker: Angela Poricelli
segments.text: Thank you, Henry.

segments.speaker: Henry Polio
segments.text: All right.

segments.speaker: Angela Poricelli
segments.text: Bye.

segments.speaker: Adam Davidson
segments.text: When you buy a few hundred pounds of fruit or vegetables, there is so much you don't know. What's the quality? How long has it been on the truck? Is the price reasonable? And it's true-- sellers and buyers who don't know each other that well, they lie to each other all the time.

segments.speaker: Adam Davidson
segments.text: So with all this uncertainty, there is tremendous economic value in long-term, trusting relationships.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Hey Adam? You're overthinking it it's so much simpler than that.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: I followed Henry from Angela's back to his booth.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: You kind of have a crush on Angela?

segments.speaker: Henry Polio
segments.text: No, I do, since I'm a kid. But she always said no.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Really?

segments.speaker: Henry Polio
segments.text: Yeah. I want to take her upstairs and she don't to.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Have you ever asked her out?

segments.speaker: Henry Polio
segments.text: No, no, no.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Does she know that you're interested?

segments.speaker: Henry Polio
segments.text: Oh, she knows. I tell her.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: You've worked next door to her for all these years and you're never been out with her?

segments.speaker: Henry Polio
segments.text: No! And I ain't going to.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Why?

segments.speaker: Henry Polio
segments.text: Because It's not the right thing to do. She's my sister.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: She's not your sister.

segments.speaker: Henry Polio
segments.text: Well, she's close to it.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: You're not with anybody.

segments.speaker: Henry Polio
segments.text: Who, me? Yeah, I got a wife.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Actually, I followed up. Henry doesn't have a wife. He did, but his marriage fell apart. And he blames the night shift for that. They never saw each other. He says all these guys here have wives they never see, kids never see.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: So I go back to Angela's, and turns out she's also divorced. She raised two boys on her own. And she says, yeah. The night shift definitely gets in the way of life.

segments.speaker: Angela Poricelli
segments.text: I remember my father. There's a lot of things he couldn't make it. On Sundays, if there was a wedding, he couldn't go. Sundays, work. My graduation, too, was on a Friday, and he couldn't come.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Really?

segments.speaker: Angela Poricelli
segments.text: Yeah. But that's OK. I understood.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: So Henry, he said you'll never go out with them because you think of him as a brother.

segments.speaker: Angela Poricelli
segments.text: Yes. I agree with him there. That I do. Plus, I'm engaged to someone right now. His name is Wayne. He's a Green Bay Packer fan.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Does he work in the market?

segments.speaker: Angela Poricelli
segments.text: No.

segments.speaker: Adam Davidson
segments.text: Does he work days?

segments.speaker: Angela Poricelli
segments.text: Days, yes.

segments.speaker: Adam Davidson
segments.text: How is it? It's hard to start a relationship.

segments.speaker: Angela Poricelli
segments.text: Very hard, very hard. It's just Friday and Saturday, really, that we see each other.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Can I check back in with you?

segments.speaker: Henry Polio
segments.text: Yeah, go ahead.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: It's one o'clock in the morning, and I'm with Henry again. He's taking a quick break.

segments.speaker: Henry Polio
segments.text: I ordered lunch, I've got Guido here, and that makes tonight.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: It's one o'clock in the morning and you just ordered lunch.

segments.speaker: Henry Polio
segments.text: Yes, yes. So everything is going smooth. Tomatoes are on fire.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Still?

segments.speaker: Henry Polio
segments.text: Yeah. We're sold out and they didn't come off the truck.

segments.speaker: Adam Davidson
segments.text: This is the point in the night where the market really changes. There are none of those people buying fancy stuff for high-end restaurants and specialty Manhattan stores. They're all gone. There's no more high-end guys like Jeff inspecting every carrot.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: A whole new group of buyers enters the market now. And they're buying for not-so-fancy places-- bodegas and grocery stores in working class neighborhoods, pushcart vendors. They're not quite as concerned with getting the best possible quality. They want a good price.

segments.speaker: Adam Davidson
segments.text: It's in this second phase that the dynamic between sellers and buyers starts to shift. Remember early in the night, when Eddie One-Way had to go searching for someone to sell him pears? Over the next couple hours, it's the reverse. The sellers are looking for the buyers. And this, says a warehouse man named Thomas Kilgaren--

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Nickname Killer--

segments.speaker: Adam Davidson
segments.text: Is the time to see who is a great salesman and who's not.

segments.speaker: Thomas Kilgaren
segments.text: There's some guys down here that couldn't sell life insurance to the Kennedys. Know what I mean? But there's some that are pretty good. If you could sell something that somebody doesn't want, that's a good salesman. I come down here looking for lettuce, you sell me lettuce-- any moron could do that. Sell me something that I don't want-- you know what? That's a salesman.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Selling something that no one wants? That is exactly what a guy named Mike Sack, Big Mike, is trying to do right now. We catch up with him toward the end of the night.

segments.speaker: Adam Davidson
segments.text: Earlier in the night, buyers were begging Big Mike to lower his prices, and he didn't. He refused. And it worked out pretty well for him. He sold a lot of Red Globe grapes and mangoes, and he made a killing in persimmons. But now that daylight's approaching, he's got piles and piles of oranges from Chile, and he's the one begging. He's pleading with one of his regular carports, a guy named Amerigo Perrera, to buy some of those oranges. Amerigo is pretty clear about his wishes.

segments.speaker: Amerigo Perrera
segments.text: No oranges.

segments.speaker: Big Mike
segments.text: You've got to give in, Amerigo, today. You've got to be nice.

segments.speaker: Amerigo Perrera
segments.text: What part of no oranges don't you understand?

segments.speaker: Big Mike
segments.text: I'll give you one pallet.

segments.speaker: Amerigo Perrera
segments.text: No! Stop playing.

segments.speaker: Big Mike
segments.text: Be nice today. Be nice in front of the camera. There's a lady present.

segments.speaker: Amerigo Perrera
segments.text: Shut up already.

segments.speaker: Big Mike
segments.text: Can I give you one for $18?

segments.speaker: Amerigo Perrera
segments.text: No, Mike, no.

segments.speaker: Big Mike
segments.text: Just be nice.

segments.speaker: Amerigo Perrera
segments.text: No.

segments.speaker: Big Mike
segments.text: Why?

segments.speaker: Amerigo Perrera
segments.text: I don't need it today.

segments.speaker: Big Mike
segments.text: One skid only.

segments.speaker: Amerigo Perrera
segments.text: Stop it, stop it, stop it. This stuff is being recorded, you understand?

segments.speaker: Big Mike
segments.text: Yeah, but they just want to see, you know, and I've give you one skid. Be nice for the microphone, Amerigo. Amerigo, one skid. How about a 56.

segments.speaker: Amerigo Perrera
segments.text: Why don't you stop playing around already? No.

segments.speaker: Big Mike
segments.text: How about a 56? Amerigo!

segments.speaker: Amerigo Perrera
segments.text: No!

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: At around 4 AM, all of the sellers in the market find themselves pretty much in the same situation as Big Mike. Tired and with too many oranges. Listen to Henry-- so tired.

segments.speaker: Henry Polio
segments.text: Oranges. Oranges are moving slow, so you know, you try to give everybody some oranges. Even if they don't want it, they're taking them. You know what I mean? Poor couple. This is, like, what time do you go to bed at night?

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: What time I go to bed? Probably like 11.

segments.speaker: Henry Polio
segments.text: So this is like your nine o'clock. You know? I hate the day.

segments.speaker: Adam Davidson
segments.text: Wait, you hate the day?

segments.speaker: Henry Polio
segments.text: Oh, I hate it.

segments.speaker: Adam Davidson
segments.text: What do you hate about the day?

segments.speaker: Henry Polio
segments.text: I don't know. The sun, everything. I get a headache. How are you, my friend? I just don't like the sun. I don't like it. I mean, I like it, but you know, like now, if the sun came up, I hate it. The morning, I ain't into. I like the dark.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: At 5 AM, Henry heads home. He rakes some leaves in the front yard, and then heads to sleep just as the sun comes out.

segments.speaker: Adam Davidson
segments.text: And later that day, a fancy grocery store in Greenwich, Connecticut might have some very nice, but kind of pricey, tomatoes. A high-end restaurant in Manhattan may be offering the chef's tomato bisque.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: But further out, in poorer neighborhoods in South Boston, Brooklyn, Queens, tomatoes will be very hard to come by. Oranges, though, will be very cheap. And there will be lots of them.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Act Two. It Was a Dark and Smoky Night.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Jenifer Hixson told this story about the random kinds of things that can happen in the middle of the night at The Moth, where people get on stage and tell personal stories in front of an audience.

segments.speaker: Jenifer Hixson
segments.text: I reached over and secretly undid my seatbelt. And when his foot hit the break at the red light, I flung open the door and I ran. I had no shoes on. I was crying. I had no wallet. But I was OK, because I had my cigarettes.

segments.speaker: Jenifer Hixson
segments.text: When you live with someone who has a temper, a very bad temper, a very, very bad temper, you learn to play around that. You learn, this time I'll play possum, and next time I'll just be real nice, or I'll say yes to everything, or you make yourself scarce, or you run. And this was one of the times when you just run.

segments.speaker: Jenifer Hixson
segments.text: And as I was running, I thought, this was a great place to jump out. Because there were big lawns and there were cul-de-sacs, and sometimes he would come after me, and drive, and yell stuff at me to get back in, get back in, and I was like, no. I'm out of here. This is great. And I went and hid behind a cabana and he left.

segments.speaker: Jenifer Hixson
segments.text: And I started to walk in this beautiful neighborhood. It was 10:30 at night. And there was no sound except for sprinklers. Ch, ch, ch, ch, brrrrr. Ch, ch, ch, ch, brrrr. And I was enjoying myself, and enjoying the absence of anger, and enjoying these few hours I knew I'd have of freedom. And just to perfect it, I thought, I'll have a smoke. And then it occurred to me, with horrifying speed, I don't have a light!

segments.speaker: Jenifer Hixson
segments.text: Just then, as if in answer, I see a figure up ahead. Who is that? It's not him, OK. They don't have a dog. Who is that? What are they doing out on this suburban street? And the person comes closer, and I can see it's a woman. And then I can see she has her hands in her face. Oh, she's crying.

segments.speaker: Jenifer Hixson
segments.text: And then she sees me, and she composes herself, and she gets closer, and I see she has no shoes on. And just as she passes me, she says, you got a cigarette? And I say, you got a light? And she says, damn, I hope so.

segments.speaker: Jenifer Hixson
segments.text: And then first she digs into our cutoffs in the front-- nothing. And then digs in the back, and then she has this vest on that has 50 million little pockets on it. She's checking and checking, and it's looking bad. She digs back in the front again-- deep, deep-- and she pulls out a pack of matches that have been laundered at least once. We open it up and there is one match inside.

segments.speaker: Jenifer Hixson
segments.text: OK. Oh my god. This takes on-- it's like Nassau. Now we've got to like, how are we going to do it? OK. And we hunker down. We crouch on the ground. And where's the wind coming from? We're stopping. I take out my cigarettes. Let's get the cigarettes ready. Oh, my brand, she says. And we both have our cigarettes at the ready.

segments.speaker: Jenifer Hixson
segments.text: She strikes once, nothing. She strikes again-- yes, fire! Puff, inhale. Mm, sweet kiss of that cigarette. And we sit there, and we're loving the nicotine, and we both need this right now.

segments.speaker: Jenifer Hixson
segments.text: Immediately we start to reminisce about our 30 second relationship. "I didn't think that was going to happen!" "Me neither!" "Oh, man, that was close!" "Oh, I'm so lucky I saw you!" "Yeah!'

segments.speaker: Jenifer Hixson

segments.speaker: Jenifer Hixson
segments.text: And we start to trade stories about our lives. We're both from up north. We're both kind of newish to the neighborhood. This is in Florida. We both went to college. Not great colleges, but man, we graduated.

segments.speaker: Jenifer Hixson
segments.text: And then it gets a little deeper, and we share some other stuff about what our lives are like. Things that I can't ever tell people at home. And she says, "Well, why don't you come back to my house and I'll give you a ride?" I say, "OK, great," and we start walking.

segments.speaker: Jenifer Hixson
segments.text: And we get to this-- lots of lights. And the roads are getting wider and wider, and there's more cars, and I see lots of stores. You know, laundromats, and dollar stores, and EmergiCenters.

It's the kind of place where you drive your car right up, and the door's right there, and there's 50 million cigarette butts outside, and there's like doors one through seven, and you know behind every single door there's some horrible misery going on. There's someone crying or drunk or lonely or cruel. And I think, oh, God. She lives here. How awful.

segments.speaker: Jenifer Hixson
segments.text: We go to the door, door number four, and she very, very quietly keys in. As soon as the door opens, I hear the blare of television come out, and on the blue light of the television, the smoke of a hundred cigarettes in that little crack of light.

segments.speaker: Jenifer Hixson
segments.text: And I hear the man, and he says, "Where were you?" And she says," "Never mind, I'm back." And he says, "You all right?" And she says, "Yeah, I'm all right." And then she turns me and says, "You want a beer?" And he says, "Who the [BLEEP] is that?"

segments.speaker: Jenifer Hixson
segments.text: And she pulls me over, and he sees me, and he says, "Oh, hey." I'm not a threat.

segments.speaker: Jenifer Hixson
segments.text: Just then he takes a drag of his cigarette and I follow the cigarette down. And I'm surprised when I see, int he crook of his arm, a little boy, sleeping. A toddler. And on the way up, she kisses the little boy, and then she kisses the man. And the man says again, "You all right?" And she says, "Yeah. I'm just going to go out and smoke with her."

segments.speaker: Jenifer Hixson
segments.text: And so we go outside and sit amongst the cigarette butts and smoke. And I say, "Wow, that's your little boy?" And she says, "Yeah, isn't he beautiful?" And I say, "Yeah, he is. He is beautiful." "He's my light. He keeps me going," she says.

segments.speaker: Jenifer Hixson
segments.text: We finish our cigarettes. She finishes her beer. I don't have a beer, because I can't go home with beer on my breath. And she goes inside to get the keys.

segments.speaker: Jenifer Hixson
segments.text: She takes too long in there getting the keys, and I think something must be wrong. And she comes out and she says, "Look, I'm really sorry. segments.speaker: Jenifer Hixson
segments.text: And she also has wrapped up in toilet paper seven cigarettes for me. A third of her pack, I note. And a new pack of matches.

segments.speaker: Jenifer Hixson
segments.text: And she tells me, "Goodbye!", and "That was great to meet you," and "How lucky," and "That was fun," and you know, "Let's be friends."

segments.speaker: Jenifer Hixson
segments.text: And I say, "Yeah, OK!" and I walk away. But I kind of know we're not going to be friends. I might not ever see her again. And I kind of know, I don't think she's ever going to be a vet.

segments.speaker: Jenifer Hixson
segments.text: And I cross, and I walk away. And maybe this would have seemed like a visit from my possible future and scary, but it kind of does the opposite. On the walk home I'm like, man. That was really grim over there.

segments.speaker: Jenifer Hixson
segments.text: And I'm going home now to my nice boyfriend, and he's going to be so extra happy to see me. And we have a one-bedroom apartment, and we have two trees, and there's a yard. So I can leave whenever I want.

segments.speaker: Jenifer Hixson

segments.text: A little while back, after we did a program that all took place at a rest stop on the side of the highway, we got an email from specialist Lindsay Freeland, who's in the Oregon National Guard, and who heard the episode by podcast from where she's stationed in Iraq. She wrote to us about the road trips that she goes on in her job, in the middle of the night, without real rest stops, to forward operating bases across the country. Quote, "It's late, it's dark, and it's not the normal to be up and driving to a destination. Here in Iraq, this is our military time for driving, late at night, due to the agreement between the American military and the Iraqi military to conduct most convoy operations at night to bring a normalcy back to the Iraqi local nationals."

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: One of our producers, Nancy Updike, reached Lindsay Freeland on the phone and learned that she's 24. Just got to Iraq in July. Started doing these convoys in August, mostly transporting fuel. There are three people in her vehicle. She's a driver. There's also a gunner and a commander. And it's so noisy that they have to talk to each other over headsets for the whole trip.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: What's amazing is how huge these convoys are-- 20 to 100 trucks, plus another 11 military vehicles providing security, which is what Lindsay's in.

segments.text: It's a pretty amazing scene. I always think of it that we're stringing through Iraq like Christmas tree lights. A bunch of white, big, bright lights snaking through the dark desert. And we usually are the biggest light out there, because not many local nationals like to drive at night.

segments.text: We conduct our operations at night. It's just our agreement so that we don't interrupt their life as much. Just because we are a really long and big convoy. So I mean, that is kind of a big deal, and that is kind of an interrupter, I guess you could say.

segments.speaker: Lindsay Freeland
segments.text: And they don't like us, and you can tell that. Because some traffic, if we're headed northbound, you know, they'll be going both ways in the southbound lane.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: So basically, they would rather cram traffic going in two directions into one lane rather than try to share the lane that your convoy's in.

segments.speaker: Lindsay Freeland
segments.text: Right, exactly. They don't want to be near us. Because we have big cruiser weapons on our vehicles. We have bright lights. We try to be nice and try to turn off the left side or something, so we dim the lights for them.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: So you're not kind of blinding other drivers.

segments.speaker: Lindsay Freeland
segments.text: Right, exactly. But usually they just don't like being near us, so they'll pull off the road completely and just turn their flashers on and wait for us to pass.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: How many of these convoys have you done?

segments.speaker: Lindsay Freeland
segments.text: Probably 20 or 30. I mean, it can get pretty mundane. Now on eight hour missions, they're like a quickie, you know, really fast.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: Because how long are the long ones?

segments.speaker: Lindsay Freeland
segments.text: The longest we've had is about 15 hours. It seems very, very long and drawn out, and your legs get pretty tired staying in that one position for a long time when you only have one stop throughout those 15 to 16 hours, you know.

segments.speaker: Lindsay Freeland
segments.text: But for the most part, we are pretty energy drink fulfilled, with a cooler next to our gunner's turret, and we just reach behind him, and grab our energy drinks. And I think I drink probably about three energy drinks in one convoy. Which is not good, you know. Not good for you. But it helps. Especially on the boring convoys, and the long, long drawn out convoys.

segments.speaker: Lindsay Freeland
segments.text: I mean, we always usually have at least one or two breakdowns of our third country national supply trucks. I think one convoy, our 15 hour convoy, what we had probably about seven or eight breakdowns. It was ridiculous.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: Is there ever a time, when you're driving or you're stopped, that you almost forget where you are?

segments.speaker: Lindsay Freeland
segments.text: Oh yeah, for sure. Sometimes I feel like I'm driving in, you know, the desert of the U.S., like Arizona or something like that. You know, it looks like a normal highway within the States. Because A, it's dark, and B, it's just a normal paved road. Yeah, it's not as kept up as well as how the states keep it up, and half the road isn't even painted where the stripes are supposed to be, but for the most part, it reminds you of a normal highway.

segments.speaker: Lindsay Freeland
segments.text: And so sometimes I feel like I'm on a long roadtrip. Sometimes I feel like I'm driving a big freight truck, like if I was a truck driver back home, you know. It's usually a pretty quick feeling, because you can be brought back pretty fast.

segments.speaker: Lindsay Freeland
segments.text: There's tires everywhere. They line the road. I mean, I'm not even kidding when I say that. Most Iraqis, they run out their tires until they're completely destroyed to smithereens, and so they'll just leave those pieces on the side of the road. There's no type of cleanup crew to come clean up the trash on the road. There's no type of officer to come pick up the destroyed tire that's in the right lane.

segments.speaker: Lindsay Freeland
segments.text: So that's usually just what seems to bring me back to being in Iraq. And then, you know, sometimes I look down-- wait, I have my body armor on. I'm in still in Iraq.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Specialist Lindsay Freeland of Alpha Company 141 with the Organ National Guard in Iraq, talking with Nancy Updike.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Act Five. Bump in the Night.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: We end our show today with this story about a very common experience-- staying up all night with a sick child. One of our producers, Jane Feltes, tells what happened to her and her parents back when she was six years old and her parents were 26. They were visiting family friends with holidays in the UP, Michigan's Upper Peninsula, which is the part of the state that isn't, you know, the mitten. Here's Jane.

segments.speaker: Jane Feltes
segments.text: This night, a lot of adults wanted to go out, so my mom volunteered to babysit about seven of us kids altogether. And all the kids' bunks were upstairs in this old, old log cabin, and the staircase to get upstairs had no railing. It was just kind of, shoots out into the middle of the room.

segments.speaker: Jane Feltes
segments.text: And I remember we all got our pajamas on, and we all ran upstairs.

segments.speaker: Jane's Mom
segments.text: And I'm not exactly sure if you slipped or got bumped by the herd of children running up the stairs--

segments.speaker: Jane Feltes
segments.text: This is my mom.

segments.speaker: Jane's Mom
segments.text: But you were falling. And I managed to grab your ankle as your head smashed into the concrete floor. From about eight feet up.

segments.speaker: Jane's Mom
segments.text: And everybody, all the kids were just frozen on the stairs. And-- ugh, this is creepy.

segments.speaker: Jane's Mom
segments.text: So I had to do something. So I'm trying to comfort you, and then you'd be crying and crying-- I mean, like, screaming. And then you'd say, oh, I'm so sleepy. You'd get really calm and still, and kind of go limp a little bit. And then you'd start screaming again.

segments.speaker: Jane's Dad
segments.text: My part, embarrassingly, was I was drinking at Pine Stump Junction.

segments.speaker: Jane Feltes
segments.text: You remember the name of it?

segments.speaker: Jane's Dad
segments.text: Pine Stump Junction. Everybody knows that place.

segments.speaker: Jane Feltes
segments.text: So that's my dad. My mom somehow piled seven kids into a car that wasn't even hers, that was sitting in the driveway, and drove us all to the bar. And she didn't know how to get there, but an eight year old in the car did, so he instructed her. And my mom and my dad, and me and my brother-- we just drove to the nearest hospital, which was in Newberry, which was a really, really tiny town in the Upper Peninsula.

segments.speaker: Jane's Dad
segments.text: And you weren't quite unconscious, but you weren't conscious. And you weren't responsive or alert. And when we got down to Newberry, it was after hours in the clinic, and night was following, and the only guy there, physician, was some retired part-time guy. Older fellow.

segments.speaker: Jane's Dad
segments.text: So I had just started practicing dentistry, and the things that were just fresh in my mind from the medical school aspect of my education-- so it was very, very scary.

segments.speaker: Jane's Dad
segments.text: wait,

segments.speaker: Jane Feltes
segments.text: Wait, what kind of stuff?

segments.speaker: Jane's Dad
segments.text: Well, like when you're looking at a patient, and they're kind of alert, and they're kind of talking, and then one of their eyes dilates, and they start to slow down and slur a little bit, and then the other eye dilates, and they're gone.

segments.speaker: Jane Feltes
segments.text: And was it happening?

segments.speaker: Jane's Dad
segments.text: No.

segments.speaker: Jane Feltes
segments.text: Oh.

segments.speaker: Jane's Dad
segments.text: No, no. But I was checking every five minutes. And I would snap my fingers and see if you were-- just because you were just listless. You just were a little while lump.

segments.speaker: Jane Feltes
segments.text: So they told my dad that they weren't even going to call a radiologist until the morning to do X-rays. And they wanted to just keep me there, overnight, like, sitting there.

segments.speaker: Jane's Dad
segments.text: And I just-- I couldn't believe that I was hearing this. That he was going to make us wait until eight or nine o'clock the next morning before we even called the radiologist. This was up in the middle of BFE, and it was at night. And I thought, this is bad. Because she could be gone by morning. And I can't do nothing overnight.

segments.speaker: Jane's Dad
segments.text: So I called the nurse in, and your mother and I talked about it a little bit, and then we called him in and said, we're taking her.

segments.speaker: Jane's Mom
segments.text: And I remember thinking, we're going to be out in the middle of the UP now. Nowhere near a hospital. In a car with a sick little girl and another little boy. And we have something like a five and a half hour drive to get home.

segments.speaker: Jane Feltes
segments.text: Home, at the time, was Ann Arbor, Michigan, where my dad went to school and where they knew there was a trauma center where if, you know, worst case scenario was happening, something could be done about it.

segments.speaker: Jane Feltes
segments.text: And I remember very little from that night, but just coming to in little flashes in the first hospital, and in the car. And I remember everything looked like I was in that movie Tron. You know, it was all very, like, black, and the edges of everything kind of glowed bright neon colors. And I wasn't walking, and I wasn't really moving much, except to throw up.

segments.speaker: Jane's Mom
segments.text: The first leg of the trip was really-- actually scary to me. Because the UP in the middle of the night-- there's no lights. There's nobody there. It's desolate. And you kind of look for lights in houses. Kind of trying to get an idea of the time. You know, our car at the time didn't have a clock in it.

segments.speaker: Jane Feltes
segments.text: Oh really?

segments.speaker: Jane's Mom
segments.text: Oh yeah. Cars didn't use to have clocks on the dashboard, and I didn't use to wear a watch. So I didn't really even know what time it was. So you'd kind of watch the windows and see if there's people up. Of course there was no traffic. I don't think we stopped.

segments.speaker: Jane's Dad
segments.text: If we did, we stopped for fuel. That's kind of a long trip. So I know we had to have stopped for fuel. But we didn't really need-- anything. Didn't need anything. There was no need to stop.

segments.speaker: Jane's Mom
segments.text: It was still really scary. I remember wondering if you were going to be trapped, somehow. Like that same little girl would be trapped with a brain injury. I mean, you couldn't walk at that point because you were so dizzy. But of course, in my mind, I'm connecting that with you can't walk. You know? Things aren't going to work anymore.

segments.speaker: Jane's Mom
segments.text: And I don't think your dad and I talked about any of that on the way home.

segments.speaker: Jane's Dad
segments.text: I worried that there was an undiagnosed spinal injury, and that you would have to fight with a wheelchair your whole life. I worried that you'd have migraines and puke all your life. Which you do.

segments.speaker: Jane Feltes
segments.text: That's true. That was one of the main lasting effects of the accident. We got to the hospital, and they did a CT scan, and found that I had what's called a contrecoup lesion in my brain. And I wasn't really able to walk for a couple of weeks. And then I didn't get back to school regularly-- I think I was out for like a month.

segments.speaker: Jane Feltes
segments.text: So that first night driving home after the accident just led to hundreds and hundreds of nights like that, where I was up all night sick. I started getting really bad migraines. I would always get them, like, two, three, four in the morning. I would wake up and I'd see these sparkly lights kind of around the edge of my field of vision. Then there's a little bit of, like, TV v static that gets bigger and bigger over the course of an hour until I'm blind. And then it's like worst-- pain so bad that it makes you throw up.

segments.speaker: Jane's Mom
segments.text: And that whole thing is like a big cluster [BLEEP]. Because you'd come in the bedroom and bend over me and say, I'm seeing those lights, Mom, I'm seeing those lights.

segments.speaker: Jane's Mom
segments.text: I do remember, as a mom, in the middle of the night when you would wake me up about that, feeling like a good mom. Because I just got up. You know? And I just remember as a kid when I was sick, a lot of times people didn't have time for that.

segments.speaker: Jane Feltes
segments.text: What do you mean?

segments.speaker: Jane's Mom
segments.text: Here's a blanket. You know? Go get a puke bowl. And kind of being sick by myself. So I know I do remember feeling good that I wasn't going to be that kind of mom.

segments.speaker: Jane Feltes
segments.text: It was nice of them to get up with me like that. But after a while, it just started to seem pointless, because there wasn't really anything that they could do to make me feel better.

segments.speaker: Jane Feltes
segments.text: My mom says when you do get up to take care of kids in the middle of the night, it can feel like you're the only people awake in the whole world. And that was true the first night, when we drove through the Upper Peninsula. And it was true for all the nights my mom got up with me. And it's true now that I have to deal with it all by myself.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Jane Feltes.
